abstract: Age-related hearing loss is accompanied by changes in auditory cortical activity, but it remains unclear which changes reflect aging itself and which depend on the loss of peripheral input. Here we compared spontaneous and sound-evoked activity in the auditory cortex of awake C57BL/6J (C57) mice, which develop early-onset hearing loss, with that of C57BL/6J x CBA/Ca F1 hybrid mice, which retain their hearing. In both strains, aging increased the irregularity of spontaneous firing and reduced the spike-timing precision of narrow-spiking neurons during natural sound presentation. In C57 mice, aging was additionally associated with a greater loss of sound-responsive neurons, increased spontaneous firing of broad-spiking neurons and more variable sound-evoked spike trains. At the level of individual neurons, the effect of sound on contrast entropy, a firing-rate-normalized measure of spike-pattern diversity, also diverged between strains with age and became negative in middle-aged and old C57's neurons. Nevertheless, population activity discriminated spontaneous, natural sound-evoked and noise-evoked conditions with high accuracy at every age in both strains. Thus, aging and hearing loss have distinct effects on the spiking of individual auditory cortical neurons, whereas population activity continues to discriminate sound conditions.
